engine.meaning: Most lines are the original word for word, so little is lost, but a few insertions bend the sense: "You mean that they didn't get on flamin' well?" turns a cautious question into an emphatic one, and "Crikey, he gets up on a chair" puts an exclamation into a neutral stage direction.
engine.sense: Several terms sit in the wrong slot: "bugger all of a housekeeper, would you say, ladies, ay?" uses "bugger all" (nothing) for "not much"; "get on flamin' well" uses an intensifier for "very well" in a question; "what would we do without the ladies, mate?" addresses women as "mate"; "Anyway, pulls his hand away" uses a discourse filler in a stage direction.
engine.authenticity: Stock tags bolted onto otherwise untouched lines: "Crikey, he gets up on a chair", "Anyway, I've not been in this house", "Now, we left in such a hurry yesterday", and "grotty bloody awful quick" stacks two words where a speaker would use one.
engine.register: Uneven: long runs are plain original ("I guess before we're through she may have something more serious than preserves to worry about."), while other lines are loaded ("I'd hate to have blokes coming into my bloody kitchen"). Swearing stays within dad level, but overall it reads lighter than a level 4 with patches heavier.
engine.tone: The play's tight, quiet menace is undercut by tics: "Crikey, he gets up on a chair" and "bugger all of a housekeeper, would you say, ladies, ay?" make the scene jokey, and Mrs Hale's "my bloody kitchen" coarsens a restrained character.
engine.flow: Joins are clunky: "Sweet bugger-all here but kitchen things", "grotty bloody awful quick", "Yeah, but nah, I don't mean anything", "Anyway, pulls his hand away, sticky".
engine.variety: Leans on a handful of fillers: "Anyway," appears three times ("Anyway, pulls", "Anyway, I've not been", "Anyway, seems mean"), with "mitts" twice and "reckon" repeated.
engine.essence: Recognisably the scene since much is verbatim ("Ah, loyal to your sex, I see."), but the inserted tics ("Crikey,", "ay?") blunt the women's quiet solidarity against the men.

yarn-dinkum.meaning: Nearly every beat survives ("the women don't crack a smile", "Not much chop as a housekeeper"), but the closing line reverses Mrs Hale's point: "that deputy sheriff who came out to get the fire going could've given this a wipe while he was at it" says he should have cleaned the towel, where the original suggests he dirtied it.
yarn-dinkum.sense: Terms fit: "has another squiz round the kitchen", "stickybeaking around and bagging the lot", "not having the place schmick". "We shot through in such a hurry yesterday" strains a little, as "shot through" usually means bolting or absconding.
yarn-dinkum.authenticity: Sounds like natural Australian speech: "Not much chop as a housekeeper", "I s'pose whatever Mrs Peters does'll be right", "Yeah, righto, Mr Henderson." Only "have a Captain Cook round the kitchen" in a stage direction feels a touch stock.
yarn-dinkum.register: A solid level 4: slang throughout dialogue and directions ("has a geek along a shelf", "keep your eyes peeled") without tipping into a yarn, and swearing kept to "Sweet bugger-all", within dad level.
yarn-dinkum.tone: The men's condescension and the women's stiff restraint survive: "laying it on like a young pollie", "the women don't crack a smile", "Seems a bit rough, bagging her". "Captain Cook" is a slightly cute touch.
yarn-dinkum.flow: Reads smoothly aloud: "He goes over to the sink, scoops a dipperful of water out of the bucket, tips it into a basin and washes his mitts."
yarn-dinkum.variety: Varied: "squiz", "geek", "Captain Cook" for looking; "bagging" appears twice ("bagging the lot", "bagging her") and "I s'pose" twice.
yarn-dinkum.essence: Clearly the scene, with its gendered sniping intact ("sticking up for the girls, I see"), though the towel line loses the women's hint that the men made the mess.

yarn-deadset.meaning: Keeps every point, including the closing hint: "that deputy sheriff that came out to light the fire might've got a bit of this on". "with the smarm of a young pollie" colours "gallantry" a shade more harshly but hangs off it.
yarn-deadset.sense: Terms fit: "Not much chop as a housekeeper", "stickybeaking around and bagging everything", "not having things schmick". The opener "Sweet bugger-all here but kitchen things" strains, since "bugger-all ... but" half-contradicts itself.
yarn-deadset.authenticity: Natural lines: "I s'pose anything Mrs Peters does'll be right", "He hops up on a chair and has a geek on a shelf", "Seems a bit rough to bag her". "MRS PETERS: Yeah, Mr Henderson." is a little casual for her.
yarn-deadset.register: Level 4 in dialogue and directions ("after another squiz round the kitchen", "washes his mitts"), a shade lighter than B in places where lines are kept close ("I've not been in this house--it's more than a year."). Swearing within dad level.
yarn-deadset.tone: The restraint and the undercurrent hold: "the women don't soften", "Course it's no more than their duty.", "Duty's all right, but".
yarn-deadset.flow: Reads cleanly ("takes a dipperful of water from the bucket and, tipping it into a basin, washes his mitts"), with the one awkward opener "Sweet bugger-all here but kitchen things."
yarn-deadset.variety: Varied slang ("squiz", "geek", "grotty", "schmick", "stickybeaking"), with "bag" twice ("bagging everything", "to bag her") and "fretting" twice.
yarn-deadset.essence: Unmistakably the scene: the men's dismissal and the women's closing ranks ("Ah, sticking up for the women, I see.", "might've got a bit of this on") carry through.

unharnessed.meaning: All beats survive and the final hint is made plain: "might've put a bit of this muck on it himself". "the men's boots on the stairs" is colour on "steps".
unharnessed.sense: Mostly exact ("Not much chop as a housekeeper", "get the lie of the land upstairs"), but "Well, wouldn't it rot your socks, women!" bends an exasperation phrase into "can you beat the women", and "sticking up for the sisterhood" is a modern term for "loyal to your sex".
unharnessed.authenticity: Natural in the main: "I s'pose whatever Mrs Peters does'll be right", "There's a fair whack of work to be done on a farm". "wouldn't it rot your socks, women!" is forced in its join.
unharnessed.register: A little light for level 4 in places, with plain lines kept ("COUNTY ATTORNEY: Yes--?", "MRS PETERS: Yes, Mr Henderson.", "Well, I don't know as Wright had either."); swearing within dad level ("here's a bloody mess").
unharnessed.tone: The tension holds: "the women don't give an inch", "Course, it's only their job.", "Seems a bit rough, bagging her".
unharnessed.flow: Smooth on the whole ("He goes over to the sink, scoops a dipperful of water out of the bucket, tips it into a basin and washes his hands.") with one awkward exclamation, "Well, wouldn't it rot your socks, women!"
unharnessed.variety: Varied ("squiz", "fair whack", "traipsing", "sticking their noses in"), though "jam" twice and "fretting"/"fussin'" recur.
unharnessed.essence: Unmistakably the scene, and the towel line keeps its quiet accusation: "might've put a bit of this muck on it himself".

yarn-troppo.meaning: Adds narrator judgements and new detail: "Serves him right for stickybeakin'", "the smarmy so-and-so", "like a young pollie after a vote", "Not a word out of 'em", "poor thing". The towel line reverses Mrs Hale's point: "could've given this a wipe while he was at it".
yarn-troppo.sense: Terms fit their context: "sticky as", "Not much chop as a housekeeper", "baggin' the whole box and dice", "havin' the place schmick". "booted out of place" overstates "shoved".
yarn-troppo.authenticity: Sounds Australian ("Up he gets on a chair, has a geek along the top shelf", "Yeah, righto, Mr Henderson."), though tags pile up: "Put it that way.", "will ya?", "are they.", "aren't they."
yarn-troppo.register: Heavier than level 4, closer to a full yarn: "Pots and pans and that.", "can't leave it alone", "the smarmy so-and-so", "have a good Captain Cook round the kitchen". Swearing within dad level ("a beaut bloody mess").
yarn-troppo.tone: The play's understatement turns into a commentator's ribbing: "Serves him right for stickybeakin'", "Not a flicker.", "off he trots". The stage directions take sides out loud, which the original leaves to subtext.
yarn-troppo.flow: Reads easily as a yarn ("Up he gets on a chair, has a geek along the top shelf, and pulls his hand back sticky as.") but leans on "And" openers in directions ("And he gives it another tug", "And off he trots", "And the women stand there", "And she straightens up").
yarn-troppo.variety: Plenty of slang, but repeats: "stickybeakin'" twice, "grotty" twice, "And" openers, and tag questions ("aren't they.", "are they.", "will ya?").
yarn-troppo.essence: Recognisably the scene, but the narrator's jeers ("Serves him right", "the smarmy so-and-so") spell out what the play leaves unsaid, flattening its subtext, and the towel line loses its barb.

engine.quote: bugger all of a housekeeper, would you say, ladies, ay?
engine.original: Not much of a housekeeper, would you say, ladies?
engine.why: "bugger all" means nothing, not "not much"; the swap is ungrammatical and the trailing "ay?" after the question is redundant.

engine.quote: You mean that they didn't get on flamin' well?
engine.original: You mean that they didn't get on very well?
engine.why: An intensifier in a careful lawyer's probing question changes its sense and register.

engine.quote: Crikey, he gets up on a chair
engine.original: He gets up on a chair
engine.why: Stage-Australian exclamation inserted into a neutral stage direction.

engine.quote: what would we do without the ladies, mate?
engine.original: what would we do without the ladies?
engine.why: Calling the women "mate" while addressing "the ladies" is a wrong-sense tag.

engine.quote: Anyway, seems mean to talk about her
engine.original: Seems mean to talk about her
engine.why: Filler "Anyway," used as a tic across the text, adding nothing.

engine.quote: Those towels get grotty bloody awful quick.
engine.original: Those towels get dirty awful quick.
engine.why: Stacked intensifiers make a pile-up, and the swear sits oddly in Mrs Hale's mouth.
Mrs Peters is deferential; a casual "Yeah" to the attorney loses that.

yarn-dinkum.quote: could've given this a wipe while he was at it
yarn-dinkum.original: might have got a little of this on
yarn-dinkum.why: Reverses the point: Mrs Hale suggests the deputy dirtied the towel, not that he should have cleaned it; the defence of Mrs Wright is lost.

yarn-dinkum.quote: We shot through in such a hurry yesterday.
yarn-dinkum.original: We left in such a hurry yesterday.
yarn-dinkum.why: "Shot through" suggests absconding; "cleared out" fits a sheriff leaving in haste better.

yarn-dinkum.quote: have a Captain Cook round the kitchen
yarn-dinkum.why: Rhyming slang in a stage direction is a little stock, after "squiz" and "geek".

yarn-deadset.quote: Sweet bugger-all here but kitchen things.
yarn-deadset.why: "Bugger-all ... but" is a clumsy construction; an Australian would say "bugger-all here, just kitchen stuff".
Mrs Peters' deference to the attorney is better kept with "Yes".

unharnessed.quote: Well, wouldn't it rot your socks, women!
unharnessed.original: Well, can you beat the women!
unharnessed.why: "Wouldn't it rot your socks" is said of a situation; tacking "women!" on makes an awkward, strained line.

unharnessed.quote: sticking up for the sisterhood, I see
unharnessed.original: Ah, loyal to your sex, I see.
unharnessed.why: "Sisterhood" is a modern, feminist-era word, odd in the attorney's mouth here.
Neutral English where an Aussie word (schmick) would fit the brief.

yarn-troppo.quote: could've given this a wipe while he was at it
yarn-troppo.original: might have got a little of this on
yarn-troppo.why: Reverses the point: the deputy is suspected of dirtying the towel, not blamed for not cleaning it.
Adds an editorial judgement to a stage direction; the play's restraint is lost.

yarn-troppo.quote: givin' her a little bow, the smarmy so-and-so
yarn-troppo.original: with a little bow to her
yarn-troppo.why: Narrator name-calling in the direction spells out subtext.

yarn-troppo.quote: laying it on thick like a young pollie after a vote
yarn-troppo.original: with the gallantry of a young politician
yarn-troppo.why: "after a vote" adds a detail the original lacks.

yarn-troppo.quote: Sweet bugger-all in here, mate. Just kitchen stuff. Pots and pans and that.

summaries.engine: Mostly the original with tags and swaps dropped in; several wrong-sense swaps and filler tics, uneven weight, and the tone of the scene suffers.
summaries.yarn-dinkum: Natural, fluent and at the right weight; one reversal in the final towel line costs meaning.
summaries.yarn-deadset: Faithful, natural and well weighted; keeps the play's restraint and its final barb. A couple of small wrinkles.
summaries.unharnessed: Faithful, tonally sound and natural, a touch light for level 4, with one strained exclamation.
summaries.yarn-troppo: Lively and natural, but heavier than asked, editorialises the stage directions, and reverses the final towel line.
